articles.title: Why India is sharing missile secrets with its private sector
articles.summary: New policy allows India’s private sector to produce advanced weaponry, supporting its goal of military self-sufficiency.
articles.body:
India has taken a major step towards opening one of its most sensitive areas of defence production to private companies.

Defence Minister Rajnath Singh approved the transfer of technologies developed by the state-run Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) for all conventional missile systems to Indian industry for domestic production, the country’s Ministry of Defence said on Tuesday.

The move marks a significant shift for the sector dominated by government-run firms and research laboratories. Private companies will be able to compete for the technology and production rights, subject to technical qualifications, certifications and other regulatory requirements, the ministry said.

The Narendra Modi-led government says the aim is to move missiles from development into mass production faster, increase domestic manufacturing and reduce India’s dependence on imports.

So, does India’s private defence industry have the capacity to manufacture sophisticated missile systems at the scale and reliability the military needs, is the country moving towards developing its own military-industrial complex, and are there security risks involved?

India’s Defence Ministry said Singh had approved the transfer of DRDO-developed technology for all conventional missile systems to Indian defence companies for production inside the country.

“The objective is to enhance domestic manufacturing capabilities, strengthen the defence industrial base, and create opportunities for the participation of Indian MSMEs (micro, small and medium-sized enterprises) and other technology partners in the supply chain,” the ministry said in a statement.

The measure would enable the “successful transition of missile system development to industrial production” and create opportunities for MSMEs and other technology partners, the ministry added.

“DRDO remains committed to working closely with Indian industry to facilitate the transfer and absorption of advanced defence technologies and to further strengthen the country’s indigenous defence capabilities.”

The announcement spans a wide range of missiles, said Aditya Ramanathan, a research fellow with the Bengaluru-based Takshashila Institution.

“It will include surface-to-air missiles, air-to-air missiles, anti-radiation missiles, antitank systems, and so on. It will also include more heavy-duty hardware like land-attack cruise missiles,” he told Al Jazeera.

India has traditionally relied heavily on state-owned defence companies to turn weapons developed by DRDO into large-scale production. Bharat Dynamics, one such state-owned company, has long held a monopoly in missile production.

Tuesday’s announcement is a “big change” because it ends that monopoly, said Ramanathan.

“Private companies have been making missile components for years, but what this decision does is allow them to move up the value chain and become prime integrators for these systems,” he said.

While India largely relies on domestically made missiles, it also imports missiles — especially from Russia and Israel, two key weapons suppliers to the country.

But under Modi, India has attempted to both encourage self-reliance in defence — a concept that the government calls Atmanirbhar Bharat or self-reliant India — and prod foreign defence majors to manufacture in India.

At a time when geopolitical allegiances are changing fast, and India faces uncertainties on both major borders — with rivals Pakistan and China — the country under Modi has more than doubled its defence budget, from $38bn in 2014 to $86bn in the current financial year.

The brief four-day conflict with nuclear-armed rival and neighbour Pakistan last year has injected fresh urgency into India’s defence preparedness plans. This year’s defence budget is 16 percent higher than the previous year’s.

Other geopolitical events have forced the government’s hand too, suggested Ramanathan.

“I don’t think this move would have happened as soon as it did if not for the experience of recent wars. Indian decision-makers have been looking at Ukraine, they’ve been looking at the US war with Iran, and of course they’ve been imbibing the lessons of operations from last year,” he said.

“One reason you’re going to need large stockpiles is that, as we’ve seen recently, you’re going to burn through your inventory pretty quickly. The other reason is that your adversary could also degrade your stockpiles using their own precision-strike systems.”

China, he said, was a major factor in India’s calculations.

“India believes that to deter China, which is its most capable adversary, it will need to demonstrate that it can both inflict and absorb really punishing attrition over weeks of gruelling warfare,” Ramanathan said.

To that end, India is also creating a tri-services conventional missile force. “To be a viable and effective force, it’s going to require serious magazine depth, and this cannot be achieved without the active involvement of the private sector,” he added.

What is India’s defence industry already manufacturing?

In June, India announced that it was preparing to spend more than $2bn on military drones from domestic manufacturers, reflecting the rapid expansion of the country’s private defence industry.

More than 600 companies were involved in India’s drone industry, including major groups such as Adani, Larsen & Toubro, and Tata Advanced Systems, as well as startups.

In July, India also approved the purchase of a range of military equipment for its defence forces worth $5.46bn, including missiles, electronic warfare systems and Kamikaze drones.

India is also pushing to rapidly modernise its navy with an eye on Beijing’s growing influence in key Indian Ocean shipping lanes. In December, New Delhi announced plans to procure at least 75 ships and submarines, with most expected to be constructed domestically.

At the same time, India is trying to diversify the foreign sources of its weapons. Over the past decade, New Delhi has worked to move away from its longstanding reliance on Russia for military hardware, expanding defence ties with countries such as the United States, France and — increasingly — Israel.

Does the private sector have the capacity to build missiles?

Private arms manufacturers in India have been increasing spending on bolstering military production in the past few years.

Major conglomerates have invested heavily in ammunition, drones, aerospace and military electronics. Of late, they have started to invest in facilities that aim to manufacture missiles.

Adani Defence & Aerospace, owned by business tycoon Gautam Adani, a close associate of Indian Prime Minister Modi, announced plans in 2024 to invest more than 30 billion rupees ($315m) in ammunition and missile manufacturing facilities in Uttar Pradesh.

The facilities would include capabilities for handling explosives used in missiles and precision munitions.

But commitments and intent don’t build missiles.

“Ultimately, I think the success or failure of this move will depend on how the Indian government places orders,” Ramanathan said. “Making missiles is an incredibly complex and costly affair, and companies are going to have to invest a lot in infrastructure, technology and people. These sorts of investments will only pay off if the government places large enough orders to justify them and also, hopefully, leave these companies with some profits that they can pour back into research and development.”

India has a range of cruise and ballistic missiles, several of which are also capable of carrying nuclear warheads.

In May, on the anniversary of the 2025 war with Pakistan, India successfully test-fired the Agni-V, its most advanced nuclear-capable intercontinental ballistic missile that can reach a distance of 5,500km (3,418 miles) — a range that covers all of China, the Middle East and even parts of Europe.

Its other ballistic missiles have ranges from as little as the Prithvi-1 (150km or 93 miles) to the Agni-IV (4,000km or 2,485 miles), again covering everything from border skirmishes with Pakistan to India’s extended neighbourhood.

It also has powerful cruise missiles, like the BrahMos, co-developed with Russia, which has a range of up to 500km (311 miles), and was used in last year’s war with Pakistan.

Is India also exporting missiles and other weapons?

India has dramatically ramped up its military exports in recent years, from just $72m in 2014-15 — when Modi came to power — to $4bn in 2025-2016.

Paras Defence, one of India’s fast-growing defence manufacturers, said this month it expects its exports to more than double in the 2026–27 financial year, up to $14m, driven partly by increased demand linked to conflicts in the Middle East.

Indian arms makers have also been involved in joint ventures with companies abroad. Adani Defence, in partnership with Elbit Systems – Israel’s largest weapons manufacturer – produces the large Hermes 900 armed drone systems.

A 2024 investigation by Al Jazeera exposed how India was exporting rocket parts and ammunition to Israel, even as the Modi government was publicly calling for diplomacy to end the war on Gaza.

In June 2026, Amnesty International said in a report that India’s weapons exports to Israel made it complicit in the genocide in Gaza.

But it isn’t just Israel that has sought and received weapons from Indian manufacturers. Nor is it just bullets and weapons parts that India is exporting today — complete missiles are in demand, too.

In 2022, the Philippines bought three batteries of the BrahMos missiles from India. Since then, Vietnam and Indonesia have signed deals with India for the purchase of these missiles. And India has submitted a proposal to the United Arab Emirates offering to supply the Gulf country these missiles, too.

Is the latest move a step towards building a military-industrial complex?

While Tuesday’s announcement marks the first time that India’s state-run research and manufacturing facilities will transfer missile technology to the private sector, the government earlier this year shortlisted private firms to manufacture the country’s next-generation fighter jets.

Tata Advanced Systems, a subsidiary of Tata Sons, and Bharat Forge are among companies to be shortlisted, and are emerging as major makers of artillery systems, ammunition and aerospace systems. India has its homegrown jets, but imports the most cutting-edge planes in its arsenal, including the Rafale fighters from France. The Indian Air Force also relies heavily on Soviet-era jets.

Still, while India “wants to build a wider defence industrial base”, said Ramanathan, “it is very far from developing the sort of military-industrial complex that [former US President Dwight] Eisenhower worried about. Power in India still resides overwhelmingly with the government.”

Despite the surge in domestic manufacturing and exports of specific weapons systems and parts, India on the whole remains a major military importer.

India was the world’s second-largest importer of weapons between 2021 and 2025, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI): Russia was its biggest source, accounting for 40 percent of India’s imported weapons.

Are there risks in transferring sensitive technology to the private sector?

As the US and Israel bombed Iran in March this year, a group of Iranian hackers claimed it broke into the servers of major US defence manufacturer Lockheed Martin, stealing blueprints of components used in the F-35 fighter jets.

The alleged data breach exposed the risks of private companies — which often have lower security standards and oversight than top-secret government laboratories — holding sensitive information.

But Ramanathan pointed out that in India’s case, “the companies that are most likely to get the missile contracts are all old hands”.

“They’ve been involved in the defence sector in some capacity for decades, and they have experience in dealing with confidentiality and secrecy,” he said.

The Indian government, on its part, also “doesn’t want the technology or its missile secrets to go to its adversaries, and it also wants to abide by its commitments to the Missile Technology Control Regime, which gives India several advantages,” he said, referring to one of the world’s major export-control regimes.

“So India has good reasons, in its own self-interest, to ensure that missile technology doesn’t leak.”

articles.title: New York City restaurants are saving 800 pounds of oyster shells from landfills every day and sending them to rebuild reefs, with 19 acres of reef habitat already restored
articles.summary: US News: New York City restaurants are giving discarded oyster shells a second life by keeping hundreds of pounds of them out of landfills every day and sendin.
articles.body: New York City restaurants are giving discarded oyster shells a second life by keeping hundreds of pounds of them out of landfills every day and sending them to a project rebuilding oyster reefs across New York Harbor. The Billion Oyster Project collects more than 300,000 pounds of shells from participating restaurants each year, equivalent to roughly 800 pounds a day. Instead of becoming waste, the shells are cleaned, cured and eventually used as a foundation for new oyster reefs. The effort is part of a much larger restoration programme that has already helped return more than 200 million oysters to New York Harbor and restore about 19 acres of reef habitat. The unusual recycling effort is turning a common restaurant waste product into material for rebuilding a lost marine ecosystem.New York City restaurants are saving hundreds of pounds of oyster shellsThe shell collection programme has created a direct link between New York Cityâs restaurants and the restoration of its harbour. Participating seafood restaurants and oyster bars separate used shells from their normal waste, allowing them to be collected and transported for restoration instead of being sent to landfill. The Billion Oyster Project says its restaurant network sends more than 300,000 pounds of oyster shells to the programme each year. That works out at approximately 800 pounds every day. The shells are particularly valuable because they can provide the hard surface young oysters need when they settle and grow. What begins as waste on a restaurant plate can therefore become part of the physical structure of a new underwater reef.The shells are cured before returning to the harbourThe discarded shells cannot simply be taken from a restaurant and placed directly into the water. They first undergo a lengthy curing process designed to remove remaining organic material and reduce the risk of introducing harmful organisms into the harbour. The Billion Oyster Project processes the shells on Governors Island, where they are cleaned and left to cure for months. The curing period can last close to a year, allowing the shells to become suitable for restoration work. Once they have been prepared, they can be incorporated into reef structures and used as substrate for young oysters. This careful process transforms what would have been food waste into a safe and useful material for marine restoration.The shells become the foundation for new oyster reefsAfter curing, the shells are used alongside concrete structures to create complex surfaces where oysters can settle. Oyster larvae need hard substrate to attach to as they develop, making old oyster shells particularly useful for reef restoration. The Billion Oyster Project seeds prepared reef material with oyster larvae before the structures are placed at restoration sites around New York Harbor. As the oysters grow, they form clusters that gradually create more complex reef habitat. The aim is not simply to place individual oysters in the water but to recreate functioning reef communities that can support other marine organisms. Over time, the restored structures can become living parts of the harbour rather than simply artificial objects on the seafloor.More than 200 million oysters have been restoredThe shell-recycling programme is one part of a much larger effort. The Billion Oyster Project currently says that more than 200 million oysters have been restored to New York Harbor. Its latest 2025 monitoring report recorded more than 180 million live oysters restored by the end of that year, showing how quickly the cumulative restoration figure has continued to grow. The organisation has also reported about 19 acres of restored reef habitat. These numbers represent years of work involving restaurants, scientists, educators, volunteers and harbour restoration teams. The project ultimately wants the restored oyster population to reach a scale at which reefs can become increasingly self-sustaining and reproduce naturally.New York Harbor once had enormous oyster reefsOyster restoration is particularly significant because oysters were once an important part of New York Harborâs ecosystem. Before large-scale urban development, pollution and intensive harvesting transformed the harbour, extensive oyster reefs covered large areas of its waters. Oysters were also a major part of New Yorkâs food economy, with the city's oyster industry once supporting enormous harvests. Over time, however, pollution, habitat destruction, overharvesting and changes to the harbour environment caused the oyster population to collapse. The Billion Oyster Project is attempting to reverse part of that historical loss by rebuilding reefs and reintroducing oysters to suitable areas of the harbour.Restored oysters can filter harbour waterOysters are more than just reef-building animals. They are filter feeders that remove suspended particles from the water as they feed. A large and healthy oyster population can therefore contribute to clearer water and improved conditions within an ecosystem. The benefits can extend beyond the oysters themselves because reefs provide shelter and surfaces for other marine organisms. The Billion Oyster Project's latest monitoring work recorded 44 different taxa of fish, crabs, shrimp and other invertebrates using restored reef areas. That suggests the developing reefs are functioning as habitat for a broader community of marine life rather than simply serving as places where transplanted oysters are kept.Oyster reefs can support coastal resilienceThe restored reefs may also contribute to New York's wider efforts to make its waterfront more resilient. Oyster reefs can absorb some wave energy and create natural habitat along coastal areas, making them an example of nature-based infrastructure. They are not a replacement for engineered flood protection, but healthy reef systems can form part of a broader strategy for protecting coastal ecosystems. Their value comes from combining several functions at once. The reefs provide habitat, support biodiversity, filter water and can help reduce the energy of waves reaching vulnerable shorelines. That makes oyster restoration relevant not only to conservation but also to the long-term environmental resilience of New York Harbor.The project has a much bigger goalThe Billion Oyster Project's name reflects its long-term ambition to restore one billion oysters to New York Harbor by 2030. The organisation also aims to involve one million students in its education programmes. Reaching that scale would represent a major increase from the harbour's current restored population and could help create conditions in which oyster reefs become more capable of sustaining themselves. The project is therefore measuring its progress through more than the number of shells collected from restaurants. It is also monitoring oyster survival, growth, reproduction and the wider communities of marine life that use restored reefs.Restaurant waste is becoming part of a living ecosystemThe most striking part of the programme is the transformation taking place between a restaurant kitchen and the harbour floor. A shell left behind after a meal might once have gone directly into the waste stream. Instead, it can now be collected, cured, placed into a reef structure and eventually become the surface on which a young oyster settles. As those oysters grow, they can create habitat used by fish, crabs, shrimp and other organisms. With more than 3.2 million pounds of shells collected so far and about 19 acres of reef habitat restored, New York City's restaurant waste is becoming an unlikely building material for bringing parts of its historic harbour ecosystem back to life.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: This prehistoric Czech sanctuary is 1,000 years older than Stonehenge; reveals how farmers tracked the movements of the Sun and the Moon 6,500 years ago
articles.summary: Rest of World News: A prehistoric sanctuary discovered near Chleby in the Czech Republic is giving archaeologists a brand new view of how Europeâs early farming communiti.
articles.body: A prehistoric sanctuary discovered near Chleby in the Czech Republic is giving archaeologists a brand new view of how Europeâs early farming communities understood the Sun, Moon and changing seasons. The circular structure, built more than 6,500 years ago, is around 1,000 years older than Stonehenge and appears to have been designed for both rituals and observing movements in the sky. According to the University of West Bohemia (UWB), archaeologists have found that the enormous enclosure contained 12 entrances whose positions were carefully arranged rather than placed randomly. Their research suggests that people who lived in the region had a detailed understanding of important solar and lunar cycles. The discovery makes the Chleby sanctuary one of the oldest monuments of its kind in Central Europe and offers a rare glimpse into prehistoric beliefs and daily life.What makes the 6,500-year-old Czech sanctuary so uniqueThe sanctuary stands near the present-day village of Chleby and dates back more than 6,500 years. As per the University of West Bohemia's report, people constructed an almost circular enclosure measuring about 230 metres across. The structure was surrounded by a ditch more than 2.5 metres deep and contained 12 entrances. What initially appeared to be a prehistoric enclosure became even more significant when archaeologists examined the positioning of those entrances. Petr KriÅ¡tuf from the Department of Archaeology at the University of West Bohemia, leads the research and explained that circular enclosures from this period are completely unknown in the region. The arrangement of the entrances therefore provided an important clue that the site had been deliberately designed. Instead of simply forming a large enclosed area, the structure appears to have been created around particular points on the horizon.Prehistoric Chleby farmers tracking the Sun and the MoonThe positioning of the entrances appears to have allowed people at Chleby to observe important events in movements of the Sun and the Moon. The research team has identified two main observation points. One is connected with the Moon's extreme positions on the horizon during its approximately 18-year cycle. The other links sunrise at the summer solstice with sunset at the winter solstice. According to the University of West Bohemia, this arrangement is similar to the better-known alignment at Stonehenge. The major difference is its age. Organic material recovered from Chleby indicates that the sanctuary was established more than 1,000 years before Stonehenge. For the farming communities who built it, these celestial events may have carried meanings beyond simply marking dates. KriÅ¡tuf said that sunrise at the summer solstice could have represented a beginning, while sunset at the winter solstice represented an ending. The layout of the sanctuary suggests that these ideas may have been built directly into the landscape.Ritualistic belief connected with the Chleby sanctuaryThe evidence suggests that the sanctuary was not simply an early astronomical observation site. Archaeologists have also discovered remains that point towards ritual activities. Bull skulls and horns were found in the ditch close to the entrances. Archaeologists believe that these remains may once have decorated large gateways leading into the enclosure. Jan Turek, an archaeologist involved in the research on behalf of Charles University, noted that the bull was an important religious symbol among Europe's first farming communities and was known from several parts of prehistoric Europe. The combination of carefully positioned entrances and animal remains therefore gives the site a more complex character. The sanctuary has connected observations of the natural world with ceremonies and beliefs. Human remains add another layer to the story. Earlier research identified a Bronze Age burial belonging to the ÃnÄtice culture. Around 18 people were buried there gradually over time.Did the sanctuary remain important for thousands of yearsAccording to the University of West Bohemia, current research suggests that its role eventually changed. By the Iron Age, the monument appears to have lost its original significance. The ditch was gradually filled in, and an ordinary settlement was established where the former sanctuary had stood. This development contrasts with the history of Stonehenge, which experienced repeated periods of renewed use and continued to acquire cultural associations long after its construction. At Chleby, the evidence points towards a gradual fading of the monument's original importance. What had once been a significant ritual landscape eventually became part of everyday settlement.Learnings from the prehistoric Czech siteThe research at Chleby is now turning particular attention to the soil surrounding and within the enclosure. Jan FiÅ¡er of the University of Hradec KrÃ¡lovÃ© is analysing soil samples because human activity can leave chemical traces even when visible objects have disappeared. According to the university, these traces could help researchers understand how the site was used during different periods of prehistory. That could reveal details that artefacts alone cannot provide. It may help establish where particular activities took place and how the use of the sanctuary changed over time. The Chleby discovery ultimately shows that sophisticated prehistoric monuments were not limited to famous sites such as Stonehenge. More than 6,500 years ago, farming communities in what is now the Czech Republic were already creating large structures whose design appears to have connected the land, the seasons and the movements of celestial bodies.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Ukraine awards Elon Musk high state honor as it seeks to expand Starlink access
articles.summary: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has bestowed one of Ukraine’s top state honors on SpaceX owner Elon Musk as ​Kyiv seeks to expand use of the company’s Starlink ‌terminals, which provide battlefield communications for Ukrainian forces.
articles.body: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has bestowed one of Ukraine’s top state honors on SpaceX owner Elon Musk as ​Kyiv seeks to expand use of the company’s Starlink ‌terminals, which provide battlefield communications for Ukrainian forces. Under a presidential decree published on the presidential website on Wednesday, Musk was awarded ​the Order of Freedom. The decree praised Musk “for outstanding ​personal contributions to protecting human life and freedom, ⁠and for developing relations between the peoples of ​Ukraine and the United States of America.” Musk switched on the ​Starlink satellite internet service over Ukraine shortly after Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. It has become the lifeblood of Ukraine’s battlefield communications ​and a tool for piloting drones. Musk agreed to ​turn off thousands of Russian “grey-market” Starlinks in Ukraine this year, causing problems ‌for ⁠Russian forces, at the behest of former Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov before he was dismissed in July. Ukraine has now asked to use Starlink over Russian territory as ​it seeks to ​attack targets ⁠including launchers for ballistic missiles that are wreaking destruction on Ukrainian cities. Zelenskyy has said ​he was told that Musk opposed the ​move ⁠as a “major escalation” of the war, but that Ukraine had “started to receive a different, more encouraging feedback.” Using Starlink over ⁠Russian territory ​could reduce capabilities that Russia ​is relying on to drag out the war, Zelenskyy said.

articles.title: Ancient Christian amulet unearthed after 1,500 years may hold biblical secret
articles.summary: Likely containing a biblical passage, a 1,500-year-old Christian amulet with a paper-thin gold sheet was unearthed by archaeologists at Türkmen Karahöyük in Turkey.
articles.body: Archaeologists in Turkey have unearthed a 1,500-year-old Christian amulet containing a paper-thin sheet of gold — and experts believe it may contain a biblical passage. The discovery, made at the Türkmen Karahöyük archaeological site in Konya, central Turkey, was reported by Turkish state media outlet Anadolu Agency (AA) earlier this summer. An international team of roughly 60 researchers from 13 countries was excavating the site when the amulet was discovered. ANCIENT CLUE CRACKS OPEN A 2,000-YEAR-OLD MYSTERY NEAR FAMED COLOSSEUM The amulet dates back to the fourth or fifth centuries A.D. — a formative time in Christian history. Inside its copper case is a thin, 0.1-millimeter gold sheet on which a passage from the Bible was "most likely" written, AA reported. It is still unclear which biblical passage it contains. Pictures show the amulet as a small, dark and heavily corroded artifact — with researchers carefully examining and cleaning it. Excavation co-director Michele Rüzgar Massa told AA that these types of amulets "are not very common." LOST PAGES WITH 'GHOST' TEXT RECOVERED FROM ONE OF THE WORLD'S MOST IMPORTANT NEW TESTAMENT MANUSCRIPTS "As far as we know, one similar example was found in Germany," said Massa, who added that the amulet likely belonged to a small child. "In other words, you can think of it like an evil-eye charm," he said. Archaeologists also found older artifacts, including a stone seal with a hieroglyphic Luwian inscription. The Luwians were an ancient people who inhabited parts of Anatolia during the Bronze and Iron Ages, and the seal dates back to roughly 1500-1400 B.C. CONSTRUCTION WORKERS CLEARING OLD BOMBS UNEXPECTEDLY FIND 'IMPORTANT' ANCIENT SANCTUARY Archaeologists also found two copper seals and a clay seal impression. Massa told AA the stone seal bears the name "Kurunti-ziti," which is linked to Kurunta, an important god in the Hittite world. "This person did not hold a very high-ranking position, but we can nevertheless see a hierarchy belonging to the bureaucracy and the state," Massa said of the person named on the stone seal. "We can say that this was a major administrative center around 1500-1400 B.C.," he added. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Deputy excavation director Hüseyin Erpehlivan told AA that the archaeological site "occupies an important place in terms of Anatolian archaeology." "Konya is located right in the center of Anatolia, in a region where cultures intersect." "Konya is located right in the center of Anatolia, in a region where cultures intersect," he said. "Türkmen Karahöyük is not an excavation focused on a single period." CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Erpehlivan added, "We are investigating a multilayered settlement extending from the Late Hellenistic period through the Iron Age and Bronze Age and into even earlier periods." The amulet is one of several remarkable finds with biblical ties to emerge from Turkey in recent months. articles.title: Iran, Oman agree on temporary Hormuz route: What we know
articles.summary: Iran’s deputy foreign minister announced a temporary shipping corridor in the Strait of Hormuz.
articles.body:
Iran and Oman have agreed on a temporary maritime route for ships travelling through the Strait of Hormuz, Iran’s Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said on Tuesday.

He, however, warned that the waterway will not fully reopen until the United States fulfils its commitments under an interim peace deal signed in June, which has since lapsed.

The US-Israel war on Iran, which began with strikes on Tehran on February 28, has effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz to shipping, sending global energy markets into crisis. The narrow waterway through which one-fifth of global oil and natural gas supplies from Gulf producers are shipped in peacetime has become a major bone of contention between Washington and Tehran, and disagreements over the critical channel continue to hinder any hopes of a lasting peace plan.

Since the US bombing of parts of Iran in July following more disputes over the strait, Iran has refused to hold direct talks with it. Even though active warfare has since paused again – replaced by a strategy of piling economic pressure on Iran – it has maintained that it will speak directly to only Oman about the future of the waterway, which passes through the territorial waters of the two countries.

Here is what we know about the new route they have agreed on.

Before the war on Iran began, more than 20 percent of global oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) shipments from the regional producers passed through the strait, which is the only sea route connecting the Gulf to the open ocean. About 130 ships crossed the strait every day. Just before the war began, the price of Brent crude – the global benchmark for oil – was about $66 a barrel.

Following the attacks on Tehran, which were carried out as talks between Iran and the US were underway in Oman, Iran closed the strait in early March, allowing only a few ships it deemed “friendly” to pass through. In April, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) issued a route map to those ships allowed to pass. This routed traffic much closer to the Iranian coast than they had previously sailed and designated a large section of Omani territorial waters as “restricted”.

The US has previously accused Iran of placing mines in the strait. While Iran has not confirmed this, it stated at the time that following its designated route would minimise the risk of encountering them.

Below is a map of the route approved by Iran in April:

The US later enforced a naval blockade of Iranian ports in and around the strait in a bid to cripple the country by restricting its fuel exports.

The war and ensuing regional tensions resulted in global energy shortages, especially in Asia where countries are particularly dependent on shipments from the Gulf, and crude prices soared. Over the course of the war, the price surged past $100 on several occasions, most recently on July 23. In March, the highest Brent crude oil price reached almost $120 a barrel.

On June 17, a memorandum of understanding (MoU) was signed between the US and Iran as they agreed to a ceasefire to facilitate peace negotiations, lasting up to 60 days. Among other measures, Iran agreed to keep the strait open for all traffic, free of charge, for 60 days. However, the vague wording of the MoU led to disagreements over which routes ships should take and the waterway fractured into two disputed routes – a southern course approved by Oman and backed by the US, and a northern one approved by Iran. The southern route is the one used by commercial carriers under US naval protection so far.

Diplomatic efforts towards a broader peace deal have since stalled and passage through the strait remains high risk.

On Tuesday, an oil tanker was disabled by an unidentified projectile close to Oman’s Ash Shishah, near the strait’s entrance, the United Kingdom’s Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said.

On Tuesday, Gharibabadi announced on state television that Iran and Oman have agreed that the entry to the new approved route will begin in Iranian territorial waters “and part of the exit route would also be through our territorial waters”.

The transit corridor will be 7 miles (11.3km) wide, he said.

However, key details remain unclear, including the precise coordinates of the route, when ships can start traversing the strait safely and how revenues would be generated.

Specific operational protocols are also not known yet, such as whether any vessels or flags will be barred from using the route.

Does this mean the Strait of Hormuz will reopen?

No. Gharibabadi emphasised that Iran has only agreed on a route for shipping with Oman, and does not consider the strait open despite the agreement on the location of a shipping route with Oman.

“The agreed-upon transit route with Oman is a temporary route,” he added.

Iranian army spokesperson Mohammad Akraminia said vessels will be subject to Iranian surveillance before they enter the strait and will only be allowed to pass if Iran grants them permission.

Gharibabadi insisted the US must fulfil its commitments under the June MoU, including granting sanctions relief and the release of frozen Iranian assets, if it wants to resume peace talks.

He urged countries to resist US pressure to place economic pressure on Iran.

US President Donald Trump announced last week the “most crushing economic operation ever” against Iran, and threatened sanctions against any country doing business with it . On Monday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent laid out a wave of new sanctions against 60 entities around the world it accuses of facilitating Iranian oil sales.

“We are urging countries not to succumb to American pressure regarding the sanctions that Washington wants to impose on us,” Gharibabadi said, adding that Washington was “mistaken about its ability to enforce its sanctions against our neighbours”.

Gharibabadi’s remarks followed talks with Omani negotiators in Tehran to finalise the details of a phased framework for the future management of the strait. Iran and Oman have been in talks for several weeks about controlling traffic through the strategic waterway.

Oman, which is known for its neutrality and position as a mediator between Iran and the US, which it considers an ally, has not publicly stated that it intends to join Iran in controlling the Strait of Hormuz.

Earlier on Tuesday, Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met his Omani counterpart, Badr Albusaidi, in Tehran to discuss the temporary navigation corridor as well as a project to clear mines, according to a joint statement.

Albusaidi said on X he hoped the countries would “soon announce” the corridor, adding that “future management of the strait and a permanent solution will follow in due course”.

Technical talks are planned to develop a long-term arrangement, including mechanisms for information sharing and navigational and security services, according to Albusaidi’s statement.

While the US has not formally responded to the news of an agreement between Iran and Oman for a shipping passage through the strait, last week Trump threatened to bomb Oman if it “gets in the way” of a peace deal between the US and Iran.

“If Oman gets in the way, we’ll bomb the s*** out of them,” he told US broadcaster Fox News on August 17. Back in May, he made a similar threat , saying, “Nobody is going to control it. It’s international waters, and Oman will behave just like everybody else, or we will have to blow them up.”

Trump also told Fox that Iran should surrender, and claimed that his administration had opened a direct backchannel for talks with the IRGC, something Iranian officials immediately denied.

On Wednesday, an IRGC spokesman told Iranian media that the US has been obstructing negotiations between Oman and Iran, leading to them being delayed.

The US and Oman are close partners with a relationship stretching back nearly 200 years.

However, an exclusive understanding between Iran and Oman over the waterway runs contrary to one of Washington’s core demands: that Iran should relinquish control of the strait as a condition of ending the war. Rather than curbing that control, such a deal would lend it greater legitimacy by formalising Iran’s position, analysts say.

But experts say Trump is also likely angry that the US has seemingly been cut out of a deal relating to the strait.

“In part, a solution mediated without US intervention and which in fact allows Oman and Iran to manage passage through Hormuz, which lies entirely within the two countries’ territorial waters, would show how impotent the United States is and has been,” Laleh Khalili, a professor of Gulf studies at the University of Exeter in the UK, told Al Jazeera last week.

The US and Iran have also strongly disagreed about whether Iran should be allowed to charge fees to shipping companies using the strait. Under international law, tolls for passing through natural waterways such as Hormuz are forbidden, even when they are not technically in international waters. However, fees for services such as insurance, environmental protection and docking can be charged. It has yet to be seen whether this issue will be addressed in the temporary agreement announced on Tuesday.

The US has long accused Iran of planting sea mines – explosives planted underwater to threaten commercial and military ships – in the Strait of Hormuz. Sea mines can include moored contact mines that detonate when a vessel strikes them, while more sophisticated “bottom mines” sit on the seabed and use sensors to trigger an explosion when they detect a ship’s magnetic or acoustic signature above.

There is no clear answer as to how many mines there are or where exactly the sea mines are in Hormuz, as Iran has not officially disclosed this. Trump has asserted that US forces have destroyed “all” 28 Iranian mine-laying boats in the strait’s international waters.

On Tuesday, Gharibabadi dismissed Trump’s claim, saying it was “only aimed at calming the markets”. He warned that US mine-detection vessels would become “very good targets” if they entered the area.

articles.title: Chinese-Eswatini relations: China advises its citizens to leave Taiwan ally over security risks
articles.summary: Eswatini is one of 12 countries, and the only one in Africa, that has diplomatic relations with Taiwan.
articles.body:
China's foreign ministry has told its citizens to leave the southern African kingdom of Eswatini over "security risks".

The ministry cited "rampant cyber fraud and criminal activities associated with gambling" as among its security concerns, but did not give details.

It suggested its citizens relocate as soon as possible to "relatively safer" countries such as neighbouring South Africa.

Eswatini is one of 12 countries, and the only one in Africa, that has diplomatic relations with Taiwan, which China claims as part of its territory.

On Tuesday, the privately owned Times of Eswatini news site reported that 40 Chinese nationals have been in detention since last month , external after being arrested while trying to leave the country.

They were first arrested - along with dozens of other foreign nationals - in March during raids on alleged illegal online gambling centres in the main city, Mbabane, and surrounding areas, the news site reported.

The group's lawyers had written to the attorney general and home affairs ministry, stating that they had pleaded guilty to immigration-related offences and had paid fines imposed by the courts, the news site reported.

The 40 were then released on the orders of the High Court, and their re-arrest was unlawful, the lawyers were quoted as saying.

The Eswatini government has not yet commented.

In its advisory to its citizens, China says those who insist on travelling to or staying in the country will face "extremely high security risks, and the timeliness of assistance may be affected".

It is unclear how many Chinese citizens work or live in Eswatini.

China has for years pressured countries to end diplomatic relations with Taiwan.

In April, Taiwan accused Beijing of trying to derail its President Lai Ching-te's travel to Eswatini by pressuring nearby countries to revoke overflight permits.

The trip, originally planned for 22-26 April to mark the 40th anniversary of Eswatini's King Mswati III's accession, was cancelled following the development.

Lai eventually travelled to Eswatini in May, without saying how he reached the country. None of the governments had announced the trip beforehand.

Following the visit, Beijing's foreign ministry said that Lai had become "an international laughing stock".

Earlier this year, China scrapped tariffs for all African countries, except Eswatini.

articles.title: Irish country stars Carlin and Buckley pay respects to Dolly Parton
articles.summary: Irish country music artists Claudia Buckley and Máiréad Carlin have been among those to pay tribute to the late country music legend.
articles.body:
Dolly Parton's death has been felt across the world since it was announced on Tuesday evening , from her native Tennesse to the village of Ventry in County Kerry, where in 1990 she stopped in for a song and a drink in a rural pub.

A booming country music scene across the island of Ireland has kept the Queen of Country as relevant today as ever, and many local talents have paid tribute to their late idol.

Irish country music artist Claudia Buckley said she was "heartbroken" to hear of Parton's death, describing the US singer-songwriter as her biggest inspiration.

Londonderry-born singer Máiréad Carlin paid her respects too, and said Parton was someone who was "beautiful inside and out".

Carlin, who performs with the all-female Irish musical ensemble Celtic Woman, once met her hero, adding: "There was no singer like Dolly".

"She paved the way for all of us to be individuals and fly our own flag in the way we want to," Carlin told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today on Wednesday.

"It was absolutely amazing meeting her, and she was everything that you could imagine her to be and more. She really was just beautiful inside and out.

"She was so tiny in person, even with her heels on. I mean, I'm 5'4" and she was about half my height."

The meeting took place alongside fewer than 10 people ahead of the premiere of 9 to 5 The Musical.

Carlin said: "She pulled us aside and told us to be true to ourselves as artists and not fold to what people expect you to be. She spoke about not putting yourself in a box.

"It was a really special moment because, for those things, when you meet people, it could've been a quick photo and move on, but she really took her time to talk to four women in the music industry."

Irish country music artist Claudia Buckley described the US singer-songwriter as her biggest inspiration.

Buckley said Parton was "a true icon" and that her music had shaped her life and career.

"The world feels a little less bright this morning. She truly was an icon and was one of the best songwriters of our generation.

"She meant so much to so many people, not just as a songwriter and a singer, but as a philanthropist and everything."

Buckley praised the Imagination Library - Parton's literacy charity - and also Parton's work during the pandemic, saying "she donated millions towards Covid-19 research".

"She has done so much for the whole world, and when an icon like Dolly dies, it is hard because you sort of feel like she would never die."

Like many fans around the world, for Buckley the death of Parton has evoked some musical memories.

"First and foremost, I am a fan. I grew up listening to Dolly, and the first song I ever learned to sing was Coat of Many Colours.

"The world will never be the same, music will never be the same, but her legacy will live on."

Parton's genre-crossing appeal saw her inducted into both the Country Music Hall of Fame and the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.

But many will remember her best for her philanthropy, which provided hundreds of millions of children with years-worth of free books.

In 1995 she established a children's literacy programme, inspired by her father Robert Lee Parton's inability to read or write.

It began as a local initiative in her home state, handing out a book-per-month to children up until the age of five, before growing into a charitable mission with an international mission.

In 2019, the Republic of Ireland became the fifth country to be helped by the charity.

The scheme was launched in Tallaght, Dublin, then in Northern Ireland in 2025 when 75 babies registered at Belfast City Hall were signed up for five years of free books.

In 1990, the patrons of a pub run by Kerry GAA legend Páidí Ó Sé, got the shock of their lives when Dolly Parton, who was holidaying in the area, gave them an intimate, impromptu rendition of one of her her biggest hits, Coat of Many Colours.

She was accompanied by Irish traditional musicians Steve Cooney and Kerry man, Séamus Beagley.

That same night, she was given a Kerry jersey by Ó Sé - a Parton gift, of sorts.

"I have that jersey in a frame, hanging in my basement, which is my recreation room," she told RTÉ Radio 1 in 2023.

articles.title: At least 14 newborns killed in Pakistan nursery hospital fire
articles.summary: Video shows grieving families at Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences after a nursery fire killed 14 infants when an AC unit compressor exploded.
articles.body: At least 14 babies at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences died in a nursery fire Wednesday, while one infant was rescued, according to hospital officials. The blaze at the major government hospital in the capital Islamabad broke out at about 6:45 a.m. after an air conditioning unit compressor exploded, hospital and rescue officials said. The fire was contained to the nursery in the hospital's gynecology ward and did not affect any other hospital wards. "One baby was rescued by a doctor," hospital spokesperson Dr. Aneeza Jalil said, adding that six of the deceased infants' bodies had been given over to families, while the remaining bodies would be given over soon. NYC 5-ALARM FIRE INJURES AT LEAST 17 FIREFIGHTERS, OTHERS AS BLAZE DAMAGES MULTIPLE APARTMENT BUILDINGS Video showed grieving families distraught with sorrow as investigators examined blasted out windows and authorities worked to secure the scene. "I don’t know what to say or whom to blame," a woman The Associated Press (AP) identified as Mrs. Mohammad Sami said. "I have lost my child," she told the outlet, just three days after she reportedly gave birth. TRUMP’S FAVORITE FIELD MARSHAL: WHO IS PAKISTAN’S POWERFUL ARMY CHIEF ASIM MUNIR WITH DEEP INTEL TIES The incident prompted Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif to remove Health Secretary Aslam Ghauri, the country's highest civil servant, from office. Sharif ordered an immediate investigation. "A tragedy involving children is an irreparable loss," he said. Shortly after the incident, Sharif convened a high-level meeting in which he expressed anger at officials for the incident and removed Ghauri. Pakistani President Asif Ali Zardari also weighed in, offering condolences to the families and saying the deaths amounted to a "heartbreaking and an irreparable loss." articles.title: Montana man who killed 4 children, 4 other family members at Sunday dinner was asked to move out: relative
articles.summary: Charlotte Ghekiere, 12, called 911 during a shooting near Billings, Montana, that left eight family members and the suspect dead, according to a report.
articles.body: A Montana man who killed eight of his relatives, including four children, during a Sunday dinner at a home in Montana had been asked by his parents weeks earlier to move out of the property, according to a family member. Brad Ireland told The Associated Press that his former wife and two children were among those killed by Alan Smith, 44, in a homicide that the Billings Police Department called an "unimaginable tragedy." Investigators said Smith died after suffering a self-inflicted gunshot wound. The victims were identified by the AP as Ireland’s ex-wife, Megan Ghekiere, and their two children, Owen Ireland, 13, and Chloe Ireland, 7. Also killed were Ghekiere’s two stepchildren with her current husband: Landon Ghekiere, 15, and Charlotte Ghekiere, 12, as well as Smith’s parents, Dana and Barb, and his grandmother Evelyn. "The one thing we do know is that Charlotte was the hero," Jennifer Mercer, a neighbor and family friend who set up an online fundraiser to help cover funeral costs and other expenses, said to the news agency. "Charlotte called 911 and she tried to save her family. And that’s something the family does want out there." MICHIGAN DAD SHOT WIFE, SIX KIDS THEN SET FAMILY HOME ABLAZE IN MURDER-SUICIDE, SHERIFF SAYS The Billings Police Department said it responded to a 911 call of an active shooting at 6:01 p.m. Sunday and heard shots fired from the back of the house. Minutes later, the property was fully engulfed in flames. Firefighters ultimately fought the blaze until around 1 a.m. Monday, according to Billings Fire Department Chief Matt Hoppel. The home is in a subdivision outside of city limits that’s not required to have fire hydrants. "Due to the condition and structural integrity of the residence, recovery and investigative efforts must be conducted carefully and methodically," the Billings Police Department said Tuesday, adding that, "we extend our sincere and heartfelt condolences to the families and loved ones affected by this unimaginable tragedy." Mercer described the family as "very loving and close," and said the children all got along and that their parents remained amicable even after divorcing. The Smith family was originally from the Seattle area. Ireland said that after he and Megan Ghekiere divorced six years ago, she moved to Montana with their children and met the man who would become her second husband, Adam Ghekiere, who was working and not at the home when the shooting occurred. She and Alan’s parents, Dana and Barb Smith, soon followed, buying a house in Billings near their daughter’s home. Evelyn Smith, their grandmother, lived in a nearby retirement community, Ireland said. Alan Smith, who also moved in with his parents in Montana, was described by Ireland as a "hermit" who spent most of his days in his room on his computer. "No one knew what he did in there 24/7," he said. DISPATCH AUDIO RELEASED IN MICHIGAN FAMILY MURDER-SUICIDE AS TROUBLED FAMILY'S SECRETS EMERGE Smith’s parents had asked Alan to move out weeks ago after he stayed with them for years, Ireland told the AP. Alan Smith had attended Eastern Washington University but had been unable to find or hold a job, the AP reported. Ireland told the news agency that to his knowledge, Alan Smith had never been violent, though he could be verbally abusive. Adam Ghekiere, who works at the airport in Billings, told the AP that he heard over a dispatch radio about an active shooting. After calling each member of his family, he raced across town to the Smith home. When he got there, the house was ablaze, and two hours later, he learned his wife and children had been killed. His children weren't supposed to be there because family dinner was usually on Friday, he said. "I don’t think he expected my kids to be there," Ghekiere said, referring to his brother-in-law. "Monster isn’t even enough to describe what he did." A GoFundMe page said Adam Ghekiere’s 15-year-old son Landon, who was set to enter his sophomore year of high school, was "looking forward to getting his driver’s license this week and was a patient, protective, and loving big brother." Funny, precocious, and adorable -- with just the right amount of stubborn -- Charlotte had an angelic smile and loved posing for pictures," it added. The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Reform proposes £30 tax rebate for HMRC phone delays
articles.summary: People on hold to HMRC for more than 30 minutes would get a tax credit under plans announced by Robert Jenrick.
articles.body:
People on hold to HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) for more than 30 minutes would get £30 off their tax bill under a Reform UK government, Robert Jenrick has announced.

Reform's economy spokesman said HMRC's treatment of taxpayers was "offensive to working people" and his party would tie the pay of senior HMRC officials to customer service targets.

To prevent abuse, the tax credit for phone delays would be limited to two occasions in a given tax year, Jenrick said.

HMRC has said it has improved its response times since a highly critical report by a committee of MPs , in January 2025, accused the organisation of seeking to "degrade its telephone service to drive taxpayers to digital channels".

The Public Accounts Committee report said nearly 44,000 customers were cut off without warning after being on hold for more than an hour in 2024 and "HMRC's treatment of taxpayers has damaged trust in the tax system".

Jenrick highlighted the findings - which were rejected as "completely baseless" by the then boss of HMRC - at a media conference in central London.

"Frankly, it is offensive to working people and I have had enough," said the former Tory MP.

"So, we will give HMRC a big incentive to actually provide proper customer service.

"I'm announcing today that under a Reform government, if you spend more than half an hour waiting for HMRC to answer your call, you will get a £30 credit off your tax bill. If HMRC delay, they can repay.

"And to make sure that the staff actually hit their targets, we'll tie the pay of senior HMRC officials to their customer service performance."

Jenrick also pledged to scrap UK privacy rules in favour of a "light-touch" approach to data protection as part of a bid to slash "red tape" for businesses.

He said the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), which mirrors EU legislation and was adopted as domestic law after Brexit, had "strangled" tech firms and small enterprises.

The framework would be replaced by rules modelled on New Zealand's privacy legislation, which Reform says has the lightest-touch regime still recognised as being "adequate" by the EU.

Labour accused Reform of wanting to "scrap vital safeguards that protect people's private data" with its "unworkable and unserious plans".

articles.body: Nepal: A sudden flood in the Bhotekoshi River battered Nepalâs Rasuwa district on Wednesday morning, sweeping through settlements and causing widespread destruction. Houses, bridges and other structures were damaged as muddy floodwaters surged through the area, with several people reported missing.Dramatic visuals circulating on social media show the scale of the flooding, with torrents of brown water rushing through communities and engulfing buildings and bridges. In some videos, structures appear to be swept away within seconds as the powerful current tears through the area. The visuals also show people struggling to move to safer ground as the floodwaters rapidly rise.The sudden surge has left large parts of the affected area severely damaged. Roads and bridges have been inundated, while homes and public infrastructure have been damaged by the force of the water. Several people are missing, although authorities have yet to release a confirmed toll of deaths, injuries or the full extent of property damage, according to The Kathmandu Post.Rasuwa Chief District Officer Narendra Pariyar said the cause of the sudden flood remained unclear. He said the weather in the area had been sunny and authorities were investigating whether the surge could have been linked to a glacier burst or another event upstream.Authorities have issued high alerts and urged residents living along the Trishuli River basin to move to safer locations. People in areas including Nuwakot, Dhading, Chitwan and Gorkha, particularly those living close to riverbanks, have been advised to evacuate as water levels in the Bhotekoshi River rise.According to a list provided by Nepalâs National Tourism Board, more than 100 Indians and 37 non-resident Indians (NRIs) are reported missing following the disaster.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Anne Donaghy: Ex-council chief convicted of two charges over email deletion
articles.summary: Her co-accused Aaron McClelland was also cleared of trying to have an email deleted.
articles.body:
A former chief executive of Mid and East Antrim Council has been convicted of two charges connected to deleting or attempting to delete an email to prevent disclosure under the Freedom of Information Act.

Anne Donaghy, 56, of Clonmore Road, Dungannon, has been fined £1,500. She was cleared of a third charge of trying to have an email deleted.

Her co-accused Aaron McClelland, of Clonmakate Road in Portadown, was also cleared of one charge of trying to have an email deleted.

The charges Donaghy was convicted of relate to an email she sent to the private email address of then-Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader Arlene Foster.

Donaghy was cleared of a charge related to an email sent to DUP councillor Greg McKeen.

District Judge Alana McSorley told the court Donaghy had been under mounting political pressure at the time she told her PA to delete the email to Foster.

She said a perception that Donaghy had been too close to the DUP "formed the basis" of Donaghy's decision to delete the email.

The judge said the "irrefutable conclusion" was that Donaghy had intended to prevent disclosure of information.

articles.title: Who was Andreethegirl? TikToker Andree Greig Baudoin dies at 39 after cancer battle
articles.summary: US Streamers News: TikToker Andree Greig Baudoin, better known online as Andreethegirl, has died at the age of 39 after a long battle with metastatic cancer. Baudoin use.
articles.body: TikToker Andree Greig Baudoin, better known online as Andreethegirl, has died at the age of 39 after a long battle with metastatic cancer. Baudoin used TikTok to openly share her life, treatment, fears, and hopes with her followers. She died on August 22 at Calcutta House by Hospice of Acadiana in Lafayette, Louisiana. After her death, a video she had recorded before entering hospice was posted on her account. In the emotional message, she said goodbye to her TikTok family and thanked them for supporting her journey.Who was Andreethegirl and why did she turn TikTok into a cancer diary?Andree Greig Baudoin became known on TikTok as Andreethegirl, where she shared personal videos about her life and cancer battle. She first created the account for her children. She wanted them to have videos they could watch later and remember her.Over time, however, TikTok became much more important to Baudoin. She described the account as her âdiaryâ and a place where she could share her feelings. Her followers watched as she went through different treatments and tried different ways to fight her cancer.Baudoin said she tried many options during her battle. She traveled to Mexico for treatment and also tried different therapies, diets, and medicines. Later, she hoped to join a clinical trial. However, she said she was told she could not take part.Her health then became much worse. Baudoin eventually learned that the cancer had progressed so much that there were no more treatments that could help her.Andreethegirlâs final TikTok message thanked her followersBefore her death, Baudoin recorded a final message for her followers. The video was later posted to her TikTok account so her community could hear her goodbye.âIf youâre seeing this video, it just means that my time has come and Iâve crossed over,â she said at the beginning of the message.Baudoin explained that she was not afraid of dying, but she was heartbroken about leaving her husband and children. She said she would never get to see her children get married, meet her grandchildren, or grow old with her husband.She also explained that she wanted to stay at home for as long as possible. But when the time came, she moved to Calcutta House. She did not want to die in her family home because she wanted the house to remain a place filled with life and memories.In her final words, Baudoin thanked her followers for loving, praying for, and supporting her. She also shared one final wish: that people should not take their health or everyday life for granted.âEnjoy the day in front of you,â she told her followers.Baudoinâs final video left a lasting message for the TikTok community that had followed her journey. Through her posts, she turned a difficult personal battle into a story that allowed others to learn from her experiences and remember her after her death.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Acceptance ran through Dolly Parton's lyrics, Newcastle PhD writer says
articles.summary: Fans from the North East and Cumbria pay tribute, including James Barker who wrote his thesis on her.
articles.body:
A man who spent five years studying Dolly Parton's lyrics for his PhD says acceptance ran through her music.

James Barker, 34, wrote his thesis at Newcastle University exploring LGBTQ+ inclusion in the country music industry, and said Parton created a "space where a lot of LGBTQIA+ listeners can hear themselves".

Tributes have been pouring in for the country music icon who died on Tuesday aged 80, including from former BBC Radio Tees presenter Stan Laundon who said she was a "bundle of fun".

Cumbrian superfan Joe Skelly, who ran her official UK fan club for many years, said she was "very, very remarkable" and planned to create a music room in his house for his hundreds of pieces of memorabilia.

Studying over the Covid-19 pandemic, Barker started each day listening to a new Dolly Parton song.

The title of his PhD took a line from her song Family: "Some are are preachers, some are gay, some are addicts, drunks and strays and not a one is turned away."

He said: "You have the explicit message of acceptance in a country song in the early 1990s.

"There's a caricature of Dolly, but the kindness she has, it's really quite genuine and deep-rooted when you listen to the songs.

"Country is an identity that's very, kind of, gatekept.

"But she created this space where a lot of LGBTQIA+ listeners can hear themselves."

Skelly, 57, from Seaton near Workington, met Parton on several occasions.

"Her gaze would be on you the whole time while you were making the point or discussing whatever subject you were talking about.

"Royalty could have walked in the room, she wouldn't have taken her gaze and her attention off you until you'd finished."

He is in the process of converting his attic into a music room dedicated to Dolly.

"I have every book ever written, I have every record ever pressed, I have every CD ever made," Skelly said.

"I have about 950 to 1,000 pieces of just physical music memorabilia.

"I'll be able to get everything out and put it in one place where I can just go and reflect."

Stan Laundon previously presented a country music show on BBC Radio Tees and managed to meet and interview Dolly Parton.

"She was a bundle of fun," Laundon said.

"A friend of mine who was with me took a photo with me and Dolly together, and he was so excited the camera was shaking and the photograph was out of focus."

He recalls asking her for an autograph but because she did not have any photos on her, she offered to send it to his address.

"Well, a couple of weeks later I got two ten by eight photographs, one signed to me, one signed to my wife."

articles.title: RB Trey Benson goes unclaimed, reverts to injured reserve
articles.summary: The fate of running back Trey Benson has been decided, as no team claimed him off waivers.
articles.body:
The Arizona Cardinals announced that they waived running back Trey Benson with an injury designation. He went unclaimed off waivers, which means he is back with the Cardinals, but has reverted to injured reserve.

What usually happens in these situations is that a player will eventually be paid an injury settlement and released from IR.

Usually, players waived in this fashion are on the mend from an injury. Benson had not practiced since before the Cardinals' first preseason game. After missing most of last season with a knee injury, from which he tried to come back from late last season and failed, he had his knee flare up again in training camp.

He is technically on the Cardinals, but his time with them is over.

It is a sad end to the promise he had as a third-round pick out of Florida State in 2024.

In two seasons, he played in 17 games and rushed for 451 yards and a touchdown, averaging 4.9 yards per attempt.

articles.title: Liverpool push for Ismaila Sarr after Minteh setback: £50m bid in, Palace player wants Anfield switch
articles.summary: Liverpool have turned their attention to Crystal Palace's Ismaila Sarr as the Reds look to sign a winger before the deadline.Liverpool have made an offer wor...
articles.body:
Liverpool have turned their attention to Crystal Palace 's Ismaila Sarr as the Reds look to sign a winger before the deadline.

Liverpool have made an offer worth around £50m for the Senegal international , after deciding against pursuing Brighton 's Yankuba Minteh .

Andoni Iraola 's side saw two bids for Minteh rejected, the last of which was around £60m. Minteh is also currently sidelined until October after undergoing ankle surgery.

Sarr has emerged as an alternative with optimism that a deal can be done. Fabrizio Romano has reported that Liverpool have lodged a £50m bid for the 28-year-old, who is keen on the move. Galatasaray had also been chasing a deal for Sarr and have had two offers turned down.

Sarr scored 21 goals in all competitions for Crystal Palace last season and was named Europa Conference League Player of the Season as the Eagles won the trophy. He then netted four times for Senegal at the 2026 World Cup this summer.

Palace are under no pressure to sell with Sarr contracted until 2029. However, the player's desire to play Champions League football and Liverpool's offer could tempt the South Londoners into a sale.

Sarr would represent a natural right-sided winger for Liverpool, following the loss of Mohamed Salah . Interest in Sarr comes alongside the pursuit of Paris Saint-Germain 's Bradley Barcola , with Liverpool keen to sign both players before the deadline.

Sarr boasts a brilliant goal record against Liverpool. He's scored seven times in 10 appearances against the Reds in all competitions for Palace and former club Watford.

articles.title: Calvin Austin injury: Giants’ WR done for season with torn ACL
articles.summary: NY Giants receiver Calvin Austin is officially done for the season.
articles.body:
New York Giants wide receiver Calvin Austin III tore his ACL, per a report from Ari Meirov of The 33rd Team .

Austin tore his ACL in a non-contact injury suffered in practice on Tuesday.

The injury is a definite blow to the Giants offense, speedy slot receiver had been having a great camp. Austin quickly developed a rapport with QB Jaxson Dart and emerged as one of Dart's favorite targets in practice. He was also emerging as one of the Giants' most explosive options, with his 4.3 speed and agility giving opposing defenders fits.

Austin was signed away from the Pittsburgh Steelers on a one-year, $1.5 million contract and looked like he might far out-play his deal.

Now his season is over before it even begins and the Giants will have to figure out a new plan for the slot receiver, and find another source of explosiveness for their offense.

articles.title: Colts edge rushers named position group to watch for potential trades
articles.summary: CBS Sports identified the Colts’ packed edge rusher room as one teams could monitor for potential trades or waiver claims before final cuts.
articles.body:
The Indianapolis Colts' depth at defensive end could make the position worth watching as the NFL's roster deadline approaches.

CBS Sports' Josh Edwards included the Colts ' edge rushers in the company of position groups around the league that could produce trade or waiver-wire targets before teams trim their rosters to 53 players.

Indianapolis has Laiatu Latu and Arden Key atop its current depth chart, with Jaylahn Tuimoloau, Micheal Clemons , George Gumbs Jr. and Caden Curry also competing for spots.

"They could, in theory, keep six edge rushers," Edwards wrote, adding that the decision could depend on roster numbers elsewhere and special teams value.

The cramped room follows an offseason in which the Colts signed Key and Clemons after Kwity Paye departed. Indianapolis has also invested heavily in young pass rushers, using a first-round pick on Latu in 2024, a second-rounder on Tuimoloau in 2025 and selections on Gumbs and Curry in the 2026 draft.

The rookies have provided nice returns so far. Curry recorded five tackles, a sack, two quarterback hits, two tackles for loss and two passes defensed in the preseason opener against the New England Patriots, while Gumbs also recorded a sack.

Indianapolis may laud that flexibility, but it could also attract calls from teams looking for help before final cuts.

articles.title: What you need to know about Nashville Predators, ViewLift streaming agreement
articles.summary: The Nashville Predators will partner with ViewLift, a product under the sports platform DAZN, for their direct-to-consumer streaming platform.
articles.body:
The Nashville Predators have announced more details about their upcoming direct-to-consumer streaming service ahead of the 2026-27 season.

On Aug. 26, the Predators unveiled a multi-year agreement with ViewLift, a streaming product recently acquired by sports entertainment platform DAZN. ViewLift will carry all non-nationally televised Predators games starting this season.

ViewLift will give Predators fans direct access to live games, on-demand replays, highlights, and original programming. It will be available on the web, iOS, Android, Apple TV, Roku TV, Fire TV, and Android TV.

Pricing and streaming plans for this new service will be announced at a later date. The service should be available to anyone in the Predators' regional viewing area, which includes Tennessee, Alabama, Kentucky, Mississippi and Georgia.

Nashville Predators 2026-27 roster with free agency additions, losses

The Predators are one of 18 professional sports franchises in the U.S. that will be carried on ViewLift.

This is the latest development in the Predators' new broadcast rights era under Scripps Sports. On April 7, the team announced a multi-year broadcast deal with Scripps, which owns NewsChannel 5 in the Nashville area. Starting this season, all non-nationally televised Predators games will appear on WNPX (Channel 28) a channel called "The Spot." According to their website , the channel is also available on cable and satellite services like DirectTV and Xfinity.
